note: The alpha ledger as data. One record per tested CLAIM (a measured relationship), not per strategy (a bundle of them). Seeded from docs/ALPHA_LEDGER.md. Records are either MEASURED (an evidence level and controls) or QUEUED (Untested, with an origin and a proposed test). Only ControlTested edges may contribute to a score; Fragile and Falsified are outcomes, not rungs. See docs/LAB_DESIGN.md. reMeasure.command carries the FLAGS, not just the verb: `xsmom` alone reproduces nothing because the default universe includes crypto and collapses the common window from 18.7 years to 3.2; `xsmom --universe equity` reproduces the recorded number exactly.

edges.title: Cross-sectional momentum
edges.claim: Rank a universe by trailing return; the top tercile outperforms the bottom over the next month.

scope.notes: 38 names tested. The crypto arm is a null but with 10 names a tercile is 3 names — underpowered rather than disproven.

decay.note: RE-MEASURED and reproduced exactly: +0.37% per 30d, sd 3.62%, 124/215 periods positive, p=0.0044 vs the recorded 0.0045 (permutation noise). Monotone by lookback unchanged: 1/4, 2/4, 4/4, 4/4.

breadth.notes: A cross-sectional basket, so the unit of breadth is the UNIVERSE, not the symbol — the rule ranks names against each other and cannot hold on one. Held on the 39-name equity universe across 8 of 8 lookbacks, monotone. The crypto universe is a null but with 10 names a tercile is 3 names: underpowered rather than disproven, so it counts as tested and not held.

edges.title: Time-series trend following — the family, not the parameters
edges.claim: A long-only trend filter on a crypto asset beats holding it, and the specific parameter values carry no information.

scope.notes: Crypto is where it earns return. On indices and gold it matches hold's Sharpe with 2-3x smaller drawdowns — crash insurance, not alpha. Long-only FX: nothing.

effect.notes: Vol-targeted BTC Sharpe 1.19 vs 0.80 hold; maxDD 23% vs 83%. ~40% drawdown for the raw version.

correlatesWith.note: same directional premise in crypto

breadth.notes: Out-of-sample multiple-of-hold on BTC. Equities and gold are recorded as crash insurance rather than as the edge holding — a drawdown property, not the claim. The family works; the specific parameters do not, and a random-parameter arm beat the optimiser.

edges.title: Asset-class polarity — crypto trends, equities revert
edges.claim: Crypto price series are positively autocorrelated at swing horizons and equity indices negatively; the correct tool family follows from the asset class.

scope.notes: USE AS A FORK, NOT A DIAL. Collinear with market depth at rho 0.96, and the sign reverses INSIDE crypto — the continuous version is mostly depth wearing another name.

decay.note: RE-MEASURED, the fork holds: crypto VR20 above 1 on 8 of 10 names, equities below 1 on the majority. Depth still tracks the split, so the caveat about collinearity stands.

correlatesWith.note: both split on asset class; check overlap before stacking

breadth.notes: 51 symbols, and the fork itself has now been reached five independent ways — POC deviation, Value Deviation, the Trading Cross, volume, and cycle translation. Breadth here means every symbol landed on the side its asset class predicts; it does NOT mean a continuous polarity variable works, which was tested and failed.

edges.title: Volume carries forward information — in crypto, and reversed in equities
edges.claim: High relative volume precedes positive forward returns in crypto and negative forward returns in equities.

scope.notes: The SIGN is asset-class dependent — this is one edge with two signs, not two edges.

effect.notes: Crypto survives in all three volume buckets with the same sign (p 0.0002-0.009); the equity arm is significantly negative.

decay.note: RE-MEASURED, signs and significance hold: crypto top-bottom volume quintile +1.26 ATR (p=0.0005), equities -0.19 ATR (p=0.0005). The asset-class sign flip is intact.

correlatesWith.note: shares the asset-class split

breadth.notes: 48 symbols, 385k bar observations. Every symbol contributes to a class-level result: crypto +1.26 ATR and equities −0.19 ATR, both p=0.0002. Breadth is full because the claim is about the SIGN differing by class, and both signs held across three independent volume buckets.

edges.title: Mean reversion to the volume POC
edges.claim: Price displaced from the rolling volume point-of-control reverts toward it over about five days in equities.

scope.notes: REVERSES in crypto — there the same displacement continues.

effect.notes: 38 symbols, 348k bars. A known anomaly; the effect is real and tiny.

correlatesWith.note: the equity half is the polarity fork restated on a specific anchor

breadth.notes: 38 symbols, 348k bars. Small but consistent; the crypto arm reverses to momentum, which is the polarity fork again rather than a failure of this edge.

edges.title: Exit on the entry signal reversed
edges.claim: Closing a position when the entry signal inverts beats a random exit with the same holding-period distribution — in crypto only.

scope.notes: The equity arm is null (0.53x, 0.84x). This is the ONLY exit rule with measured skill; every mechanical exit tested worthless.

breadth.notes: BTC 32.34x (p=0.003) and ETH 4.35x (p=0.034) against a random same-length exit. SPY and QQQ are flat null (0.53x, 0.84x) — this is a crypto-only edge and the breadth says so.

edges.claim: US equities drift upward in the days before a scheduled FOMC announcement.

scope.notes: Four US equity vehicles, same offset, same sign, 224 real dates.

effect.notes: DECAYED: three of four vehicles have lost 70%+ of the effect post-2015 and XLF has gone slightly negative.

breadth.notes: Four US equity vehicles at the SAME offset with the same sign, which is what makes it credible. Gold and crypto show nothing. Note the decay: roughly 70% of the effect is gone post-2015, so breadth here is a pre-publication number.

effect.unit: R (random entries under the same filter: 0.007R)

edges.title: The Trading Cross z-score rule
edges.claim: Long when the rolling z-score of price crosses above +1, flat when it crosses back below 0.

scope.notes: 10 of 10 crypto assets beat hold; 0 of 3 traditional. What it does is AVOID DRAWDOWN, not time entries.

correlatesWith.note: a trend filter in z-score clothing; heavily overlapping exposure

breadth.notes: 10 of 10 crypto names beat hold; 0 of 3 traditional. The cleanest breadth split in the registry, and the reason this is scoped crypto-only. It is drawdown-avoidance rather than return generation.

effect.notes: Monotone and significant against a naive baseline — and 0.00 ATR (p = 0.9855) against a matched price/SMA baseline on the same rows.

edges.claim: CPI, NFP, PPI and GDP release days carry an exploitable directional edge.

edges.claim: Assets oscillate on a countable cycle of a characteristic length that can be traded.

effect.notes: 200 surrogate series built by shuffling log returns reproduce the cycle length on every asset, landing inside the claimed band. It is a property of the detector, not of the market.

edges.title: Cipher confluence (oscillator + tape + structure)
edges.claim: Requiring three orthogonal Cipher components to agree produces high-conviction entries.

effect.notes: Structure labels tested indistinguishable from random; SR proximity was a 15-bar lookahead. The components are not orthogonal — they are transforms of the same price series.

edges.title: The Hurst exponent classifies assets as trending or mean-reverting
edges.claim: Hurst separates trending assets from mean-reverting ones and can route the strategy choice.

effect.unit: Hurst range across all 17 asset/timeframe combinations (0.57-0.60)

edges.claim: A sentiment gate on a technical entry improves it.

effect.unit: the gated spec was byte-identical to the ungated one

edges.title: A confidence model over price features
edges.claim: A gradient-boosted model over price and indicator features ranks setups usefully.

effect.notes: Stable and calibrated, not a coin flip — and below the threshold that justifies building on it. Asset-tuned models were WORSE. What signal exists lives in regime/vol features, not in the indicator signals.

edges.title: Fibonacci retracement levels are respected
edges.claim: Price respects Fibonacci retracement ratios more often than it respects arbitrary levels drawn on the same swings.

scope.notes: BTC across four timeframes, ~355,000 level tests. Levels go live with the same delay a real trader has (a pivot at bar p is only knowable at p+span).

effect.notes: THE NUMBER THAT EXPLAINS THE FOLKLORE: a RANDOM horizontal line is respected 59% of the time. 'Levels hold about 60% of the time' is true of ANY line — it is a property of the measurement geometry, not evidence the level did anything. Fib confluence does show +4.4% for crowded zones, but random lines reproduce 2.6 of those 4.4 points: crowded zones are ranges, and ranges keep ranging.

correlatesWith.note: same failure shape — a confluence effect that a density/random control reproduces

edges.title: A bullish engulfing weekly candle predicts the next week's direction
edges.claim: After a bullish engulfing weekly candle, the following week closes higher more often than it closes lower — and enough more often to justify trading only that direction all week.

scope.notes: THE CHEAPEST TEST IN THE VIDEO: one directional claim, weekly bars, a stated prior, no discretionary inputs. The control is the base rate of up-weeks for the same asset — an asset that closes up 55% of weeks unconditionally makes a 55% conditional hit rate worthless.

effect.notes: Equities -2.31 pts, 11/39 instruments positive, 0/39 significant where ~2 were expected by chance. Crypto +3.21 pts but 5/10 positive and the era split kills it: H1 +10.4, H2 -1.8. The cheap alternative (last week simply closed up) is flat everywhere too, so there is no plain weekly momentum either.

origin.who: Davi (Lithuanian FX trader), Titans of Tomorrow interview
origin.quote: if I see that the previous weekly candle is bullish engulfing it's more likely than not that the next week is also going to have more bullishness than bearishness ... is there a chance the next candle is bearish? yes, but it's way lower chance

edges.title: Position size should scale with multi-timeframe agreement
edges.claim: Trades taken when weekly bias, daily structure and the zone all agree have higher expectancy than trades taken when they conflict — enough to justify sizing 6% versus 1%.

scope.notes: THE UNTESTED CORNER. Twenty edges in this registry and not one is about SIZING. The claim is a conditional-expectancy test: bucket trades by how many timeframes agree and compare per-trade R. Watch for the tautology trap — if the bias filter and the entry are derived from the same price series, agreement is partly arithmetic.

effect.notes: Null, and THE OVERLAP CHECK IS THE FINDING: 'close above the 50-bar mean' is true at 100.0% of entries against a 23-30% base rate, because a z-score cross upward mechanically implies it. That condition cannot discriminate between entries, so '3 of 3' is really '2 of 2'. With that understood equities are flat (+0.313/+0.308/+0.349 across buckets) and crypto is non-monotone with the MIDDLE bucket best. Neither survives a random-subset null. FIRST MEASUREMENT THIS LAB HAS MADE ABOUT SIZING. HONEST LIMIT: one entry on daily bars, versus his 5-minute entries under weekly/daily/30m structure.

correlatesWith.note: same shape — a higher-timeframe regime filter conditioning a lower-timeframe entry

origin.who: Davi (Lithuanian FX trader), Titans of Tomorrow interview
origin.quote: some of analysis is not just for me to decide if I'm going to buy or sell but it's more like me shaving off risk ... if everything is in structure everything is bullish, beautiful zones, I'm going to risk more; if there's things that doesn't tick the box I'm shaving off my risk

edges.title: How price approaches a level predicts whether the level holds
edges.claim: A level approached by one-way momentum holds less often than one approached in a two-way, alternating fashion; and a level price has ranged around for a long time holds less often than one approached cleanly.

scope.notes: CHEAPEST REAL TEST WE CAN RUN — the respect harness (RespectCommand, LevelRespectAnalyzer) already measures whether a level holds, with surrogate controls. This adds one conditioning variable. Note the internal tension in the source: he shaves risk on one-way momentum INTO the level, yet says he prefers aggressive approaches over price hanging around the level. Both halves are separately measurable.

effect.notes: Every daily bucket is a null; the largest real-vs-random difference is -1.2 pts at p=0.708. Real levels DO hold less after loitering (47.5% -> 42.7%) and random lines do exactly the same, so the conditioning describes the measurement. Baseline: real levels 46.2% vs random lines 46.7% -- real levels are not better than random lines at all, which independently reproduces the fib finding under a different respect definition. A 4h crypto arm shows three of six buckets at p<0.05 with inconsistent signs; recorded, not believed.

correlatesWith.note: MUST reuse that study's control — a random line is respected 59% of the time, so any conditional respect rate is meaningless without the matched random-level arm

origin.who: Davi (Lithuanian FX trader), Titans of Tomorrow interview
origin.quote: if it's slowly approaching my supply or demand there's no momentum against me, I'm going to continue to hold full risk ... if the price is just going crazy into my supply and demand, momentum is against me, I'm going to shave off my risk. Also I don't like when the price hangs around my liquidity too long because that ranging is just accumulation of stop losses

edges.claim: Supply/demand levels formed during an instrument's primary sessions (London/New York for EURUSD) are respected more often than levels formed outside them.

scope.notes: Cheap: tag each level by the session it formed in, then compare respect rates — the existing respect harness with one extra column. Confound to control: session also determines volatility and volume, so match on those before claiming the session did anything. BLOCKED ON DATA 2026-08-01: the claim is about FX sessions and this lab holds no FX snapshots. Crypto trades continuously so a session tag there tests something else. Needs an FX intraday source before it can be run.

correlatesWith.note: same harness, same random-level control required

origin.who: Davi (Lithuanian FX trader), Titans of Tomorrow interview
origin.quote: if I'm trading EURUSD I'm only looking for liquidity in London and New York session ... people make a big mistake where they're looking for EURUSD liquidity inside of Asian session

edges.title: Sweep and reclaim: breach equal highs, then close back inside the range
edges.claim: Entering when price breaches a cluster of equal highs/lows and then CLOSES back inside the range beats entering on the breach itself, and beats a random entry at the same moments.

scope.notes: Algorithmically definable, which most of this video's 'liquidity' language is not: equal highs within a tolerance, a breach, a close back inside within N bars. Two controls needed — random entries at the same timestamps, and the same entry WITHOUT the reclaim requirement, which isolates the part he says matters.

effect.notes: Not supported. The one arm resembling the claim -- crypto daily, +0.754 R for waiting -- is the SMALLEST sample (n=241) and is contradicted by both larger ones: on crypto 4h both real arms underperform random entries, and on equities the difference has the wrong sign at a fortieth of the size. Even at face value, almost all of the crypto-daily gap is the breach arm being bad (-0.637 vs a -0.137 random floor) rather than the reclaim being good: waiting avoids a poor entry rather than creating a good one, which is the polarity finding restated -- do not short a crypto breakout.

origin.who: Davi (Lithuanian FX trader), Titans of Tomorrow interview
origin.quote: you have series of equal highs, a move up, and then back into the range — that move back into the range is a confirmation of my entry ... I need the closed candle, not the open candle

edges.title: A fixed 1:3 reward-to-risk target maximises accumulated profit
edges.claim: Over many trades a fixed 1:3 target accumulates more profit than 1:1, 1:2 or 1:8 — with a small runner left on beyond it.

scope.notes: DIRECTLY CONTRADICTS our exit finding, which is what makes it worth running. We measured that fixed-percentage scale-outs destroy 95-100% of the return because the R-distribution has a fat right tail — but that was CRYPTO DAILY. His market is intraday FX and indices. The real question underneath is not '1:3 or not' but 'does the fat right tail exist in intraday FX at all?' Measure the R-distribution FIRST, per asset class, then the target choice answers itself. Note he keeps a 10-20% runner at breakeven, which is a hedge against exactly the tail we measured.

effect.notes: Falsified in both classes. Total R rises monotonically 1:1 through 1:8 and letting the signal decide beats every fixed target: crypto +3.265 R/trade vs +0.155 at 1:3, equities +0.321 vs +0.134. The distribution says why before any target is tested -- the median trade LOSES (-0.75R) and the top 10% of trades carry 101% (crypto) and 245% (equities) of total R, so in equities the other 90% collectively lose money. Extends EXIT_FINDINGS: the fat right tail is not a crypto peculiarity. HONEST LIMIT: his market is intraday FX with 15-pip stops and we have no FX data; this shifts the burden rather than settling it.

correlatesWith.note: the crypto arm of this question is already answered and the answer was NO — so run this as an asset-class fork, not as a fresh question

origin.who: Davi (Lithuanian FX trader), Titans of Tomorrow interview
origin.quote: I tried my strategy with 1:1, 1:2, 1:8 over hundreds of trades. 1:3 is my ideal ... 1:3 had the best, not the win rate, but best profit when it's accumulated over many trades

edges.title: Stopping after consecutive losses improves results
edges.claim: Stopping for the day after two consecutive losses, and for the week after four, improves outcomes.

scope.notes: Has a clean prior test: if trade outcomes are serially INDEPENDENT the rule cannot change expectancy, only variance — so measure the autocorrelation of trade outcomes first. If it is zero, the rule is behavioural rather than statistical, which is a legitimate reason to keep it and a dishonest reason to claim an edge from it.

effect.notes: No statistical basis: outcomes are serially independent, slightly negative if anything, so a stop-after-N-losses rule cannot move expectancy -- only variance. That makes it a BEHAVIOURAL rule, which is a good reason to keep it and a dishonest reason to claim an edge from it.

origin.who: Davi (Lithuanian FX trader), Titans of Tomorrow interview
origin.quote: if I have two losses in a row I'm done for the day, and if I have four losses in a row I'm done for the week

edges.title: A 0-1 'risk metric' from price extension over its own history
edges.claim: A composite normalised to 0-1 from price relative to its long-term moving averages, rank-scaled over the asset's own history, identifies high-risk and low-risk zones better than the plain price-over-SMA distance it is built from.

scope.notes: Benjamin Cowen's rainbow risk metric, as a general construction rather than his exact undisclosed formula. THREE TRAPS TO BUILD AROUND, all of which this project has already been bitten by. (1) LOOKAHEAD: normalising over the FULL history uses the future to rank the past — every published rainbow chart does this. Must be an EXPANDING-WINDOW percentile using only prior data, which is what makes the honest version look far worse than the picture. (2) THE BASELINE: the metric IS a price/SMA transform, so the only meaningful test is whether the composite beats its own simplest component — the exact control that killed MVRV (matched price/SMA baseline gave p = 0.9855 where the raw signal gave 0.0002). (3) SAMPLE SIZE: on BTC the whole claim rests on three cycles, and a diminishing-returns correction fitted to those same three cycles is retrospective selection, not evidence.

effect.notes: THE LOOKAHEAD PREMIUM IS 2.3x: ranking against the whole series (what a published rainbow chart shows) gives a 6.9-point spread in crypto; ranking against prior data only, which is all a trader can do, gives 3.0. More than half the picture's apparent power comes from knowing the future. The 0-1 normalisation then adds almost nothing over its own raw input (3.0 vs 2.6 for plain log price/MA) -- the same control that killed the on-chain metrics, landing the same way. Equities are a null with the WRONG SIGN (-0.8 pts, high-risk decile has higher forward returns, 2 of 9 steps monotone), which is the asset-class polarity finding reappearing. What remains is a weak crypto signal that is mostly 'price is far above its 200-day average', across three cycles.

correlatesWith.note: same shape and probably the same fate — a normalised valuation band that must be run against a matched price/SMA baseline on the same rows
built from the same price-over-long-MA information

origin.who: Benjamin Cowen (risk metric / rainbow chart)
origin.quote: PARAPHRASE, no transcript captured: a 0-1 risk value per asset, rendered as rainbow bands, built from price relative to long-term moving averages and normalised over the asset's history with a diminishing-returns correction for later cycles.

edges.title: A bearish engulfing weekly candle precedes a down week in crypto
edges.claim: In crypto, the week after a bearish engulfing weekly candle closes down more often than that asset's unconditional down-week rate.

scope.notes: FOUND WHILE TESTING THE OPPOSITE. The bullish claim from the video is dead; its mirror was free to test and is the only arm that survived anything. Consistent with this project's repeated finding that crypto's two directions are not mirrors of each other.

effect.notes: Cheap-alternative control (plain down week) is +0.04 pts, so the structure is doing the work and not momentum. Era split holds and strengthens: H1 +5.2, H2 +12.0. THREE REASONS IT IS NOT ESTABLISHED: four pooled tests were run so the Bonferroni threshold is 0.0125 and 0.013 sits just outside; the ten crypto instruments are not ten independent samples because they move together, which narrows the pooled null dishonestly; and 209 signals is a small base.

correlatesWith.note: the same study; this is the mirror arm of the falsified claim

edges.title: The surprise moves price, not the scheduled date
edges.claim: Post-earnings returns scale with the earnings SURPRISE (actual minus consensus EPS), even though the release DATE itself carries no directional edge.

scope.notes: THE FOLLOW-UP THE MACRO STUDY EARNED. Release dates for CPI/NFP/PPI/GDP tested null while FOMC did not, and the proposed explanation was that FOMC is a policy ACTION while CPI/NFP are DATA the market spends the interval forecasting -- so the surprise should move price rather than the date. That was untestable while macro consensus was paywalled. It is testable on EARNINGS: Alpha Vantage's free EARNINGS endpoint carries reportedEPS, estimatedEPS and surprise back to 1996 (verified 2026-08-01). Controls needed: post-earnings drift is a documented anomaly, so the arm that matters is whether surprise MAGNITUDE ranks forward returns beyond the plain event-date effect, plus an exposure-matched null on the drift window.

effect.notes: NULL on both halves. The surprise does not rank forward returns: quintiles are non-monotone at every horizon with Q2 the best, not Q5, and the beat-minus-miss spread is +0.08% over 20 bars, +1.11% over 60, +0.51% over 120. The event itself adds nothing over plain exposure either: +0.14 pts of level at 20 bars, and NEGATIVE at 60 and 120 (-0.14, -0.13) against the same stocks' own returns over any equivalent window. SAMPLE CAVEAT, and it is a serious one: 10 mega-cap US names (AAPL CAT CVX IBM JNJ JPM KO MCD MMM MSFT) are the most analyst-covered stocks in the market, which is exactly where post-earnings drift is weakest by construction. The literature finds it in small caps with thin coverage, which this universe has none of.

correlatesWith.note: this is the surprise-side test of the same hypothesis that the date-side test falsified
the action-versus-data distinction these two together are meant to settle

origin.who: this project's own macro/FOMC contrast (2026-08-01)
origin.quote: PARAPHRASE of our own MACRO_EVENT_FINDINGS conclusion: FOMC is a policy action and CPI/NFP are data the market spends the interval forecasting, so the surprise should move price, not the date.

edges.title: A ladder that is always in the trend's direction
edges.claim: Opening a position after N volatility clicks in one direction, with a trailing stop, and reversing on every stop-out, so there is always a trade open while price is moving, beats holding.

scope.notes: Cody's idea, formalised: click = fraction of ATR so rung spacing breathes with volatility; N clicks to open, K-click trail, reference resets on stop-out.

effect.notes: Loses money nearly everywhere: beats hold on 3/10 crypto and 1/41 equities, and beats its own random-parameter arm on 4/10 and 1/41. THE ALWAYS-IN PART IS WHAT BREAKS IT -- long-only is 4x better in crypto (2.39x) and 7x better in equities, and the short side helps on 1 of 10 crypto instruments. Sixth independent failure of a symmetric short here. NOT COSTS: with costs set to zero it still loses at every rung width from 0.5 to 4.0 ATR, the free and cost columns landing within a few points of each other. Widening rungs improves equities only by trading less and converging on holding, and still returns a quarter of what doing nothing did.

correlatesWith.note: the long-only variant IS this edge; the ladder's new ingredient is the always-in reversal, which is the part that fails

origin.who: Cody
origin.quote: if price goes in a certain direction for a number of clicks it opens a trade so long as price goes in that direction with a trailing stop so no matter the direction there is always a trade open so long as there is trend

edges.title: Market-on-close imbalance moves the index into the closing print
edges.claim: The notional dollar imbalance of market-on-close orders predicts the index's move into the closing auction, with roughly $400 million of net imbalance being the threshold that starts to move the S&P.

scope.notes: HIS ACTUAL EDGE, and the first claim in this series that is STRUCTURAL rather than pattern-based: a floor seat shows him the closing-bell order flow at 14:00 ET while the public sees it at 15:50. That specific advantage is information LATENCY and is not replicable by us at any price. What IS testable is the weaker public version: does the imbalance published at 15:50 predict the 15:50-to-close move, or the next open? BLOCKED ON DATA -- MOC imbalance is a paid exchange feed, not available free. Note also that the mechanism is well documented in the microstructure literature, so a positive result here would be replication rather than discovery, and the question is whether anything survives at the public dissemination time.

origin.who: Peter Tuchman (NYSE floor broker since 1985), Titans of Tomorrow interview
origin.quote: for every $400 million there is notional dollar value to buy or sell it will affect and move the market ... at 2:00 in the afternoon my handheld computer populates with all the orders for the closing bell ... at 3:50 this information goes out to the public

edges.title: The 15:00 and 15:30 moves are worth following rather than fading
edges.claim: US equity indices make a directional move around 15:00 and 15:30 ET, and being on the same side of that move outperforms fading it.

scope.notes: TESTED 2026-08-02 and FALSIFIED, once an Alpaca key unblocked US equity intraday. SPY/QQQ/IWM/DIA/AAPL, 5-minute SIP bars 2016-2026, ~2.2M bars. THE CONTROL THE RECORD DEMANDED -- every hour of the session measured the same way -- is what settles it: the 15:00 window's continuation rate is 50.03% against 50.25% across the other hours, ranking 4TH OF 7. Mean follow-through correlation across every hour is +0.0014, two orders of magnitude below Narang's 0.03-0.04 for a SUCCESSFUL strategy. Hannan's time-of-day claim (cleaner moves at the open, poor follow-through at 1pm) is folded into this record and also fails: open 50.87% vs 13:00 49.91%, and the open's follow-through CORRELATION is the most NEGATIVE of the session, so its two halves point opposite ways. WHAT IS TRUE: the volatility smile is real -- mean absolute move IS largest at the open and into the close. So 'the market makes a big move at 3' is correct about MAGNITUDE and carries no directional information. The claim conflates volatility with predictability, which is easy to notice from the floor and requires counting to falsify.

effect.notes: Sign-flip null with a 50% expectation. Mean follow-through correlation across all hours +0.0014. Costs not modelled -- unnecessary for a null, but a positive result would have needed them.

correlatesWith.note: same proposed mechanism -- this is the retail-observable shadow of the imbalance flow

origin.who: Peter Tuchman (NYSE floor broker since 1985), Titans of Tomorrow interview
origin.quote: at 3:00 and at 3:30 usually the market make a big move ... your retail audience should know that you should rather be on the same side of the move that the market does at 3 and 330 rather than trying to be counterintuitive

edges.title: Market regimes now flip too fast for the traditional labels to mean anything
edges.claim: Since 2020 the persistence of trend and volatility regimes has shortened enough that terms like bull market, bear market and recession no longer describe distinguishable states.

scope.notes: TESTED 2026-08-02 and FALSIFIED. Regime = a confirmed percentage swing at theta = 10% (correction) and 20% (textbook bull/bear); a mechanical label rather than a journalist's, because his anecdote is about how the PRESS used the words. Each instrument's history is tiled BACKWARDS from today into slices of exactly the post-COVID length, so the short recent window is never compared against a fifty-year mean. The post-COVID era ranks 3rd of 8 for flip rate at both thresholds. The reason the claim FEELS true: the era immediately before it (2013-10 to 2020-02) is the calmest six years in the fifty-year record -- 17.5% vol against 22-32% elsewhere, and the longest mean regime duration of any era -- so a trader comparing the last six years against the six before them correctly sees regimes half as long. The baseline moved, not the market.

effect.notes: Raw p 0.456 (theta 10%) and 0.546 (theta 20%); both controls land at or below zero (+0.7% / -3.0% vs shuffled surrogate, -7.7% / -6.1% vol-scaled). Mean rank of the recent era 3.0 and 2.8 out of 8 eras. Moving the era boundary six months to exclude the COVID crash FLIPS the sign of every arm, which is decisive against the claim. Design p-floor is 1/(number of slices) = 0.125, stated in the output.

origin.who: Peter Tuchman (NYSE floor broker since 1985), Titans of Tomorrow interview
origin.quote: you cannot use a term like a bull market and a bare market ... when in January we were down 1400 points at 11:00 a.m. and the press was talking about oh my God we are now in a bare market ... and then the market reversed and by 2 o'clock in the afternoon we were actually in a bull market ... when you have something that historically used to take generations now happening over lunch, you need to re-evaluate these things

edges.title: Pyramiding by recycling the same dollar risk beats a fixed position
edges.claim: When a trade develops structure allowing a tighter stop, move the stop up and add size to return to the SAME dollar risk. Repeated across a trend this converts a $10k initial risk into a position worth many multiples of it, without ever increasing the amount at risk.

scope.notes: TESTED 2026-08-02 and FALSIFIED, by the cleanest margin in the ledger. Entry and exit held FIXED (z-momentum in, signal out); only the size schedule varied across five arms. TWO CONTROLS, both decisive. (1) STRUCTURE CARRIES NOTHING: the pyramid is indistinguishable from adding at RANDOM moments inside the same trade with the same add count -- equities +2252.0 R vs +2251.0 R, a difference of one R across 41 instruments, 19/41 favouring the pyramid. (2) IT LOSES TO PLAIN LEVERAGE: holding the same average position flat from entry beats it on 41/41 equities and 6/6 crypto, 47 of 47 with no exceptions. The mechanism is visible in hindsight -- a pyramid buys LATER at WORSE prices, so it carries a higher average entry than a flat position of the same average size, which owns the whole move rather than the back half of it at a premium. WHY THE BELIEF SURVIVES FROM THE INSIDE: the pyramid DOES beat flat 1x (1.03-1.12x), so a trader who pyramids genuinely makes more than one who does not. The comparison never made is against the same trader simply sizing up at entry. Re-run with a loosened exit (--exit-z -1.0, 34-37 bar holds) to give the technique its best case; the verdict did not move.

effect.unit: percent shortfall (2252.0 R vs 3052.2 R, equities, long-hold arm)
effect.notes: Loses to the leverage control on 47 of 47 instruments. Beats flat 1x by 1.03-1.12x, which is the number that makes it persuasive and the wrong comparison. Structure vs random adds: 19/41 equities, 2/6 crypto -- a coin flip.

origin.who: David Hannan / 'Laptop Legend' (full-time trader ~4.5 years, small-cap short seller), Titans of Tomorrow interview
origin.quote: you might have had a 10K initial risk on a trade, but you just get so big after adding and moving your stop up that that 10k initial risk turns into a million dollars ... it's not necessarily increasing risk, it's recycling the same risk

edges.title: The first red day after a parabolic run is a short
edges.claim: After several consecutive up days with expanding range, expanding volume and gaps, the first day that breaks the prior day's low reverses, and the more extended the run the better the odds.

scope.notes: His single most-repeated setup and fully mechanical: N consecutive up days + expanding true range + expanding volume + gap-ups, then enter on the break of the prior day's low with the run's high as the stop. He also gives the transfer rule -- it is a small-cap pattern that only works on large caps 'when large caps start behaving like small caps', which is itself a testable conditioning statement rather than hand-waving. CONTROLS: the extension is measured against a base, so define the base algorithmically with a fixed confirmation lag or the setup is retrospectively selected. Compare against a random-entry short on days matched for the same trailing return, because 'stocks that ran a lot then fell' is what mean reversion IS and the question is whether the volume/gap/range conditions add anything. Survivorship cuts the WRONG way here for once -- the snapshot universe excludes the parabolic names that never came back -- so a null would be conservative and a positive result would be optimistic. Our own rubber-band finding says mean reversion is real in equities at ~5 days and REVERSED in crypto, so a crypto result of the same sign as equities would be the surprise.

origin.who: David Hannan / 'Laptop Legend' (full-time trader ~4.5 years, small-cap short seller), Titans of Tomorrow interview
origin.quote: when you get a large cap that gets really really overextended and starts behaving like a small cap where you get three four five up days in a row with expanding range and volume and they're gapping up each of those days, that's when you can actually bet big

edges.title: Mean reversion has a higher win rate than breakouts
edges.claim: Fading a parabolic extension wins more often than trading a breakout, even though the breakout carries better reward-to-risk.

scope.notes: Stated as fact -- 'it's a fact if you go look at the data' -- and cheap to check, which is exactly the kind of aside this pipeline exists to catch. Both arms must be defined mechanically and given the SAME risk unit and the SAME horizon, or the comparison is between two different trades. Report win rate AND mean R side by side: his own framing is that he accepts the lower win rate for the better payoff, so a result where breakouts lose more often and still earn more would CONFIRM him rather than refute him. That asymmetry has to be stated before the test runs, not after.

origin.who: David Hannan / 'Laptop Legend' (full-time trader ~4.5 years, small-cap short seller), Titans of Tomorrow interview
origin.quote: normally I like breakouts, but they do inherently have a much lower win rate than a mean reversion type strategy if you know how to time it correctly

edges.title: Ascending triangles break up and descending triangles break down
edges.claim: A flat resistance with rising support resolves upward; a flat support with falling resistance resolves downward; symmetrical triangles are roughly 50/50.

scope.notes: Queued specifically because the terminal is gaining an opt-in chart-pattern DESCRIBER, and the standing policy is describe freely, score never. This is the claim that would have to be true before any pattern readout could carry a directional hint -- so testing it decides whether the feature stays purely descriptive. THE PRIOR IS BAD AND SHOULD BE STATED UP FRONT: every price-derived pattern claim tested in this project has come back null (random horizontal lines respected 59% of the time, real swing levels 46.2% against 46.7% for random, fib ratios nothing across 355,000 tests). The control that matters is the DETECTOR surrogate -- run the same triangle-finder over return-shuffled random walks, because a rule that finds converging trendlines will find them in noise. He also volunteers that the symmetrical case is 50/50, which is a usable internal control: a detector with no information should produce the same rate for all three.

origin.who: David Hannan / 'Laptop Legend' (full-time trader ~4.5 years, small-cap short seller), Titans of Tomorrow interview
origin.quote: when you get ascending support and like a flat resistance line I tend to think that's going to break up to the upside ... and then you can get the symmetrical ones where to me it's a little bit more 50/50

edges.title: Swing candidates should be ranked by average daily range
edges.claim: A swing book built from high average-daily-range names outperforms one built from low-ADR names, because a 2% ADR stock cannot move a portfolio the way a 7-8% ADR one can.

scope.notes: Sounds obvious and is not, because it is a claim about RETURNS and the mechanism offered is about RANGE. High-ADR names deliver more of both directions, so the null is that ADR ranking buys volatility and nothing else. The decisive control is volatility-normalisation: compare high-ADR and low-ADR books at MATCHED risk (position sized to 1 ATR), where the range advantage is removed by construction. If the high-ADR book still wins at matched risk the claim has content; if it does not, this is a leverage statement wearing a selection statement's clothes, and the cheaper answer is to size up on the low-ADR names.

origin.who: David Hannan / 'Laptop Legend' (full-time trader ~4.5 years, small-cap short seller), Titans of Tomorrow interview
origin.quote: if you're focusing on stuff with a 2% average daily range it's just not going to meaningfully move your portfolio like something with a 7 8% average daily range would

edges.title: Analyst revision breadth leads price
edges.claim: Rank a universe by the month-over-month change in the bullish share of its analyst rating mix; the top tercile outperforms the bottom over the following month.

scope.notes: QUEUED BY THE EARNINGS NULL. Surprise tested null on 10 mega-caps and the write-up said why: post-earnings drift lives in thinly covered small caps and every name tested was among the most analysed securities in existence. Revision breadth is a claim about the ANALYSTS rather than the number they missed, so if coverage is what kills surprise, coverage is what this needs. RUN 2026-08-02 AND NOT ANSWERABLE: FMP's free tier caps grades-historical at 10 rows per symbol and blocks some symbols outright, leaving 11 names and 6 usable monthly cross-sections. Minimum detectable effect 6.47% per month (~78%/yr) against a literature effect well under 1%/month, so the observed -1.56% spread (t=-0.68) is noise and must NOT be read as a null. Fixed by `grades record` monthly (~3 years) or a paid tier. Universe is also wrong for the hypothesis: all mega-caps, no thin coverage.

correlatesWith.note: same universe, same coverage confound — both are about whether analyst attention leaves anything on the table

origin.who: queued by the earnings-surprise null, 2026-08-02
origin.quote: A null here is consistent with the effect not existing and equally consistent with the effect existing where analysts are not looking.

edges.title: Weekly cycle lows are spaced more regularly than chance
edges.claim: Weekly cycle lows occur at a consistent 28-35 week spacing (average ~31), and each weekly cycle decomposes into three daily cycles plus one inversion.

scope.notes: DISTINCT from camel-cycle-counts, which tested the DAILY cycle length and found it reproduced by shuffled surrogates. This is a claim about the regularity of SPACING at the weekly level and about the 3-dailies-per-weekly decomposition, neither of which was tested. The band he states is tight (28-35 weeks, enumerated as 31/32/28/35/32/28) which makes it falsifiable. HARD REQUIREMENT: the labelling rule must be fixed in advance with a confirmation lag -- he revises the count as price arrives, using 'inversion' and 'failed cycle' as escape hatches, so adopting his live count would test his judgement rather than the system.

correlatesWith.note: same source system; the daily-cycle LENGTH claim from it is already Falsified as a detector artifact, so any test here must not reuse that detector

origin.who: Camel Finance, daily market update
origin.quote: all of these weekly cycles are pretty equally spaced apart ... spaced between 28 and 32 weeks with an average of about 30 or 31 weeks

edges.title: A late cycle high predicts a faster, deeper decline
edges.claim: When a cycle's high prints late in the cycle (right translation), the subsequent decline into the next cycle low is faster and deeper than after an early high.

scope.notes: The one genuinely new and mechanically testable claim from this source, and it is a CONDITIONAL SHAPE claim rather than a timing claim, which is why it survives the objection that killed the cycle counts. Strong prior against: our own cycle work already found translation is momentum in cycle vocabulary and splits crypto/equity like everything else, so the cheap alternative -- 'what went up fast comes down fast', i.e. plain trailing return -- must be a named control arm. Also needs phase-randomised surrogates, since the detector that defines the cycle was itself shown to manufacture cycle lengths.
